items.title: ASTRA
items.text:
Agentic Schema for Transparent Research Analysis is a YAML specification for scientific analyses. Code captures execution, but not the full structure of an analysis: astra.yaml records the inputs, outputs, methodological choices, and evidence behind an experiment, making the work easier to reproduce and extend.

Agents are expanding the scale and speed of science, which shifts the bottleneck from producing results to trusting them. astra.yaml gives each experiment a structured record for agents to follow, keeping assumptions, choices, and evidence explicit.

ASTRA is intentionally agnostic to the execution harness so that agents, workflow runners, and humans can all read and act on the same spec.

Get started Read the specification

Alpha development

ASTRA is in early alpha. The schema, CLI, and tooling are all still moving — expect breaking changes between minor versions, and pin the schema version in your analyses. Bug reports, design challenges, and use cases that the spec doesn't yet cover are exactly what we want to hear at this stage; please open an issue on the GitHub repo, join the Community tab, or come help define the schema at the Agentic AI 4 Science Developer Summit.

items.title: Why ASTRA?
items.text:
Scientific results depend on methodological choices: which data to include, how to handle outliers, which prior to assume, and so on. In ordinary research code, those choices are often scattered across notebooks, scripts, comments, and memory. This makes results hard to reproduce, audit, and expand.

ASTRA gives every methodological choice an explicit place in the spec. In ASTRA, decisions name the options that were considered, link to evidence, and feed into a universe, which records the results for a given set of choices.

items.title: At a glance
items.text:
In ASTRA, an analysis declares the design space, a universe picks one option per decision it uses, and the CLI allows for validation and inspection. Below is an example of an astra.yaml. For the full format, see the specification.

Analysis (astra.yaml)Universe (astra.yaml)Run it 
spec_version: "0.1.0"
label: Period-Luminosity Fit

inputs:
  catalog_data:
    path: data/catalog_data.csv
    description: Periods and mean apparent magnitudes.

outputs:
  fit_params:
    type: table
    format: csv
    description: Slope, intercept, and scatter for the fitted relation.
    inputs: [catalog_data]
    decisions: [fit_method]
    recipe:
      command: >-
        python src/fit_period_luminosity.py
        --catalog {inputs.catalog_data}
        --method {decisions.fit_method}
        --out {output}

decisions:
  fit_method:
    label: Fitting method
    rationale: The fitting method determines how outliers influence the inferred relation.
    options:
      ordinary_least_squares:
        label: Ordinary least squares
      robust_linear:
        label: Robust linear fit

# astra.yaml, continued
universes:
  baseline:
    description: Default configuration for the period-luminosity fit.
    decisions:
      fit_method: ordinary_least_squares

uv tool install astra-tools

astra validate
astra info
astra plan

GitHub PyPI (astra-tools)

items.title: About ASTRA
items.text: ASTRA stands for Agentic Schema for Transparent Research Analysis. It is a declarative format for describing scientific analyses in a way that is precise enough to drive automated execution and transparent enough to be audited, reproduced, and revisited.

items.title: Who builds it
items.text: ASTRA is developed by Lightcone Research. We write most of the code today, but ASTRA is intended to grow into a community-owned standard — we are looking for collaborators across disciplines and tooling stacks to help shape it.

items.title: Open source by design
items.text:
The position paper that motivated ASTRA argues that the substrate for agentic-era scientific records cannot live behind a vendor wall. We agree, and we are committed to keeping ASTRA open in three concrete ways:

  • Open licenses. The schema is released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under BSD 3-Clause. Both permit unrestricted commercial and academic use.
  • Open development. All work happens on public GitHub repositories — issues, discussions, and pull requests are visible from the first commit onward. There is no parallel private fork.
  • Open governance, eventually. As ASTRA stabilises beyond alpha, we will move it into a community-governed structure (steering group, public RFC process, version-decision protocol). The current Lightcone Research stewardship is a starting point, not the long-term home — see Governance and the RFC process for the model we are growing into.

If you would like to help shape that trajectory — through code, schema review, downstream tooling, or simply by trying ASTRA on a real analysis — see the Community page.

items.title: Citing
items.text:
If you use ASTRA in your work, please cite the GitHub repository — the easiest way is the "Cite this repository" button on the astra-spec GitHub page, which produces APA and BibTeX entries from the CITATION.cff at the repo root. Include the schema version you targeted (it is recorded in the $comment of each generated JSON Schema and of rules.json).

The canonical namespace for ASTRA is https://w3id.org/astra/.

For the broader argument that motivates the project — agentic-era science, per-result trust, and why an open substrate matters — see the Lightcone Research position paper (a separate citation; not a replacement for citing ASTRA itself).

items.title: CLI reference
items.text:
astra is the command line of astra-tools. It validates ASTRA analyses, shows what they plan to build, and checks what was built against its records. It reads ASTRA 0.1 files; ASTRA 0.0.x files need the 0.2 line of astra-tools (Installation).

astra runs no recipe. A runner, such as lightcone-cli, builds the results and writes their records, and astra reads them.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• PATH is an analysis's folder, the current folder by default. Nothing is searched for: the analysis is the astra.yaml in that folder, the root of its stack.
  • Exit codes:
    • 0 when the command answers;
    • 1 when the analysis breaks a MUST, a planned result isn't unchanged, or what was asked for isn't there;
    • 2 for a usage error, an analysis that can't be read, a broken environment (a paper that can't be got, a folder that can't be written, git or the cache unusable), or an internal error.
  • Output. Problems are grouped by file, one per line, as line:col level CODE message. Each code is a rule of the specification, listed under Rules, or one of astra-tools' own three, which astra rules lists. astra paper verify adds two warnings of its own. NO_COLOR turns colour off.
  • JSON. validate, plan, view and check take --json. Each JSON document names its shape, such as astra-validation-report/1, and a shape changes only under a new name.
  • The cache keeps the commits fetched from remotes, the validity of analyses from a commit, the hashes of files, the checkouts runners make for their runs, and papers. It sits outside every repository, and everything in it is safe to delete. ASTRA_CACHE_DIR, an absolute path, moves it.
  • astra --help, and --help after any command, give each command's options. astra --version gives astra-tools' version.

The examples come from a small analysis, line-fit. It declares another analysis, noisy-line, at a commit, and fits a line to noisy-line's points two ways: by least squares, in a universe ols, and by the Huber loss, in a universe huber. Its comparison reads both fits.

items.title: Commands at a glance
items.text: Command What it does astra init Make a minimal analysis astra validate Validate an analysis and its whole stack astra info Show the stack in brief astra universe List the universes, or show one's selection astra plan Show the planned results, their places and commands astra view Show the analysis as it is in one universe astra check Check the records and bytes of the planned results astra history Show what git holds of a result's records over time astra rules List the rules, or show one astra spec Describe the fields of ASTRA files astra schema Show or export the JSON Schemas astra guide Print the guide for agents astra paper Keep cited papers, and seek quotes in them astra cache Show or clear the cache astra completion Print a shell completion script

items.title: astra init
items.text:
astra init [DIR]

Makes an astra.yaml in DIR, the current folder by default, with a spec_version and one output. Where no git repository holds DIR, it becomes a new one. Exits 2 where DIR already has an astra.yaml.

$ astra init my-analysis
Made my-analysis/astra.yaml, in a new git repository.
Check it with: astra validate my-analysis
$ cat my-analysis/astra.yaml
spec_version: "0.1.0"
outputs:
  result:
    type: metric
    format: json
    recipe:
      command: python src/result.py '{output}'

items.title: astra validate
items.text:
astra validate [PATH] [--json] [--offline]

Checks every parse, schema and validator rule (Rules) over the whole stack: the analysis in PATH and every analysis it declares, at their commits. It reads no results; astra check does. Exits 0 when the analysis is valid and 1 when it breaks a MUST. A SHOULD that is broken is a warning and doesn't change the exit code.

Option Meaning --json Print the report as JSON (astra-validation-report/1) --offline Fetch nothing: use only the commits already in the cache

An analysis declared by url and commit is fetched into the cache, once.

$ astra validate
astra.yaml
  4:11 error MISSING_INPUT_FILE `data.csv` names no file, and no stand-in of Git LFS, git-annex, DVC
  10:17 error UNRESOLVED_ADDRESS `method` names nothing: this analysis has no decision `method`
astra.yaml: invalid, 2 error(s), 0 warning(s)

items.title: astra info
items.text:
astra info [PATH]

Shows each analysis of the stack, the root first, with its declarations, inputs, outputs, decisions and universes. A switch shows the decision it switches on and its cases. It checks nothing, and prints text only.

$ astra info
astra.yaml
  analyses  noisy: astra.yaml at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d from file:///…/noisy-line
  outputs   fit: table, json
            comparison: table, json
  decisions method: ols, huber
  universes ols
            huber
astra.yaml at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d from file:///…/noisy-line
  inputs    config: config.json
  outputs   points: data, csv

items.title: astra universe
items.text:
astra universe list [PATH]
astra universe show UNIVERSE [PATH]

list names the analysis's universes, and the universes it imports from other analyses. show gives a universe's effective selection (Elements): each decision with the option selected, and, where the option is inherited through derived_from, the universe it comes from.

$ astra universe show huber
huber
  method: huber

items.title: astra plan
items.text:
astra plan [PATH] [--json] [--notes]

Lists every planned result, each after what it reads. For each result it shows where its record and its bytes go (Results), the folder its recipe runs in, the resources the recipe asks for, if any, and its command with the placeholders filled in (Elements). A result that belongs to an analysis from a commit isn't built here: it is read through its record at that commit (Results).

Option Meaning --json Print the plan as JSON (astra-plan/1), with every note --notes List each note, not only how many there are of each kind 
$ astra plan
points
  record    .astra/records/points.json at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d
  bytes     results/points.csv at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d
  read through its record at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d
fit#ols
  record    .astra/records/ols/fit.json
  bytes     results/ols/fit.json
  run in    .
  command   python3 src/fit.py ols 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d:results/points.csv results/ols/fit.json
fit#huber
  record    .astra/records/huber/fit.json
  bytes     results/huber/fit.json
  run in    .
  command   python3 src/fit.py huber 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d:results/points.csv results/huber/fit.json
comparison
  record    .astra/records/comparison.json
  bytes     results/comparison.json
  run in    .
  command   python3 src/compare.py results/ols/fit.json results/huber/fit.json results/comparison.json
4 planned result(s)

A path written <commit>:<path> names a file in that commit, as git names it: the runner gets the bytes and gives the recipe a path to them.

The notes point out things that are valid but easy to miss. None of them is a breach:

  • a pin that names another analysis's universe only because its own file has no universe of that id;
  • a result with two names;
  • an output with no planned result;
  • an output that isn't built in some universe, because a switch it reads has no case there for the option selected, and a switch that nothing reads with no such case (Elements);
  • results that are one computation in several universes;
  • a command that names a path outside its analysis's folder, or inside a folder below it that holds an analysis of its own.

The text counts and lists only the pins, outputs and commands that concern what the analysis in PATH builds: a pin that a planned result reads through, and the outputs and commands of the analysis and of the analyses its universes drive. A line gives the whole stack's count where it is more.

items.title: astra view
items.text:
astra view UNIVERSE [PATH] [--json]

Shows the analysis as it is in UNIVERSE. For each analysis of the stack, it gives whether that analysis is built in UNIVERSE (Elements); the option selected for each decision, or that the universe doesn't use it (Results); each output's result and where it goes, or why it has none; and the case each switch takes. --json prints it as astra-universe-view/1. Exits 2 where the analysis has no universe UNIVERSE.

$ astra view huber
universe huber
astra.yaml  built
  method       huber
  fit          fit#huber  results/huber/fit.json
  comparison   comparison  results/comparison.json
astra.yaml at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d from file:///…/noisy-line  built
  points       points  results/points.csv at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d

items.title: astra check
items.text:
astra check [PATH] [--at REV] [--json]

Checks each planned result's record and bytes, at each of its places (Results):

  • the record is unchanged, stale (something it was made from has changed since) or missing;
  • the bytes are present (the ones the record gives, at their default place) or absent.

Then it gives each evidence the status of what it cites. A stale result comes with the reasons. Where the analysis breaks a MUST, its errors come first, and only the results they leave determined are shown. Exits 0 when every planned result and evidence is unchanged, and 1 otherwise.

Option Meaning --at REV Check the analysis as it is at the commit REV names, with its records and bytes there --json Print the report as JSON (astra-check-report/1)

Here the huber universe has been edited to select ols, and nothing has been built since:

$ astra check
.astra/records/points.json at 18cfe9d5695d7fc13a3d93bbbba2f6a644bd284d  points  unchanged  present
.astra/records/ols/fit.json  fit#ols  unchanged  present
.astra/records/huber/fit.json  fit#huber  stale  present
  error STALE_RESULT `method` selects `ols` in `huber`, where it selected `huber` at 3b70b4352de6
.astra/records/comparison.json  comparison  stale  present
  error STALE_RESULT `fit#huber`, which it reads, is stale
astra.yaml
  53:19 error STALE_EVIDENCE `comparison` cites `comparison`, whose record is stale
astra.yaml: 4 place(s) of planned results, 2 unchanged, 2 stale, 0 missing; 0 absent

An input whose content is kept outside git, behind a stand-in (Elements), is compared by the hash the stand-in gives. astra-tools recognises Git LFS pointers, git-annex links and DVC files, and fetches none of them. Other packages, a runner say, can add their own stand-ins through the entry-point group astra.standins.

items.title: astra history
items.text:
astra history timeline ADDR [PATH]
astra history lineage ADDR [PATH] [--used-by]
astra history get ADDR@REV [PATH]
astra history find (--hash H | --environment IRI) [PATH]

Reads a result's records over time, from git. ADDR is a result's address, as its record gives it (fit#ols, comparison), which astra plan lists. A record's versions are its file at each commit along HEAD's history that changed it. Exits 1 where the analysis breaks a MUST or what is asked for isn't in git, and 2 where ADDR names no planned result or REV names no commit.

Command What it shows timeline ADDR Each version of the result's record, newest first: the commit that changed it, and the hash, size, commit, end and environment it gives lineage ADDR What the result was made from, as its record at HEAD gives it, down to the input files. With --used-by, the planned results whose records list it instead get ADDR@REV The bytes the result had at the commit REV names (a commit, a branch, a tag), checked against its record there, written to standard output find The versions of planned results' records whose bytes have the hash H (sha256:<hex>), or whose environment is IRI. It takes one of the two options, not both 
$ astra history timeline 'fit#ols'
fit#ols  .astra/records/ols/fit.json

    bytes        sha256:83a2d44052552a981f0bb7d48cfb46827494634183a606dcbf6a1ad6eaedac4f, 84 byte(s)
    made at      a1889b94c7b1625919f63acf9dd95347b10b45c9
    environment  urn:astra-examples:cpython-3.14
  40f49da033b761882429561e49160d3bb143ee92
    bytes        sha256:d266a39423ab53320599471891c4500987b46580e9e6546291e829d7d643e33f, 84 byte(s)
    made at      f0766da472d7b359f747994823af57a8491a32e0

{

items.title: astra rules
items.text:
astra rules [CODE]

Without CODE, lists every rule of the specification by layer, with its code, level and statement, and then astra-tools' own three. With CODE, in any case, shows that rule, with its layer and level (and astra-tools, for astra-tools' own) and, for a check rule, its status when broken.

$ astra rules MISSING_INPUT_FILE
MISSING_INPUT_FILE
validator, MUST
An input's `path` names a file (no symlink, folder or gitlink) or a stand-in

items.title: astra spec
items.text:
astra spec [TERM]

Describes the fields of ASTRA files, from the specification's schema. Without TERM, it lists every class, enum and type with its first sentence. With TERM, in any case, it shows a class, enum or type in full, a field of every class that has it, or one field as Class.field.

items.title: astra schema
items.text:
astra schema show NAME
astra schema export FOLDER

The JSON Schemas of ASTRA files, as astra-spec ships them: analysis for astra.yaml, provenance for a record, and provenance.open for a record of a later minor version. show prints one; export writes all three into FOLDER as NAME.schema.json.

items.title: astra guide
items.text:
astra guide

Prints astra-spec's guide for agents, llms.txt, as it is.

items.title: astra paper
items.text:
astra paper add DOI [--version N] [--file PDF] [--email ADDRESS]
astra paper list [PATH]
astra paper verify [PATH]
astra paper seek DOI QUOTE... [--version N] [--page N]

Keeps the papers that an analysis's evidence cites by DOI in the cache, and seeks its quotes in them (Elements), or quotes you give. A quote is sought within the page its location gives (page=6), or in the whole text. For verify, a paper not in the cache (EVIDENCE_PAPER_MISSING), or a quote not found (EVIDENCE_QUOTE_NOT_FOUND), is a warning, never an error.

Command What it does add DOI Keeps the paper of DOI. An arXiv DOI (10.48550/arXiv.<id>) is fetched from arXiv, at --version where given; any other from the open-access copy Unpaywall knows, which asks for --email. --file keeps a PDF you have instead. Exits 2 where the paper can't be got or isn't a PDF list Lists each work the analysis's evidence cites by DOI, and whether its paper is in the cache verify Seeks each quote the analysis's evidence takes from a work it cites by DOI. Exits 0 whatever it finds seek DOI QUOTE... Seeks each QUOTE in the paper of DOI that add kept, as verify would, with no analysis: within --page where given, or in the whole text. Shows the pages each quote is found on, which a location such as page=6 can give. Exits 1 when a quote isn't found, and 2 where the paper isn't in the cache or has no page --page

items.title: astra cache
items.text:
astra cache path
astra cache clear

path prints the cache's folder. clear deletes what astra keeps there, and leaves anything else in that folder alone.

items.title: astra completion
items.text:
astra completion bash|zsh|fish

Prints the shell's completion script. Load it from the shell's startup file:

  • bash, in ~/.bashrc: eval "$(astra completion bash)"
  • zsh, in ~/.zshrc: eval "$(astra completion zsh)"
  • fish, in ~/.config/fish/config.fish: astra completion fish | source

items.title: Community
items.text:
ASTRA is an open project, intentionally early. The schema, tooling, and documentation are all developed in the open on GitHub, and the most valuable thing the project can have right now — while it is still in alpha — is contact with people who are actually trying to use it.

If you find ASTRA useful, awkward, surprising, missing something, or just adjacent to a problem you care about, the project wants to hear from you.

items.title: Where to find us
items.text:
Channel Use it for astra-spec issues Schema bugs, proposed schema changes, doc issues. astra-tools issues CLI bugs, validator issues, paper-cache problems. GitHub Discussions Open-ended questions, design conversations, "is this the right approach?" threads. RFCs Significant or contested changes — new schema concepts, breaking changes, versioning rules, conventions. Pull requests Code, schema, and documentation changes — for both repositories.

When in doubt about which repo to file an issue in: schema or specification questions go to astra-spec; CLI / validator / paper-tool questions go to astra-tools.

items.title: What's most useful right now
items.text:
In alpha, three kinds of contribution are worth more than they will be later:

  • Real-analysis attempts. Take an analysis you actually ran and try to express it in ASTRA. Report what fits, what doesn't, and where the spec forced you to invent a workaround. These reports are the single best signal for what to fix at the schema level.
  • Schema review. Read the specification and the field reference with an adversarial eye. Ambiguity, missing constraints, and clashing names are easier to fix now than after the format has consumers.
  • Downstream tooling experiments. Build something that consumes an ASTRA spec — a runner, a renderer, a retrieval index, a JSON-Schema-driven editor. Even a prototype tells the project what is awkward to consume, which is information the spec authors otherwise don't have.

Documentation fixes, typo PRs, and tightening of error messages are also welcome and small enough to ship the same day.

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
The full guide is in CONTRIBUTING.md. The short version:

  1. Open an issue first for anything non-trivial. It gives reviewers context and avoids parallel work. For significant or contested changes, that issue is also the first step of the RFC process.
  2. Keep changes focused. A schema change, a doc change, and a tooling change are three separate pull requests.

  3. Run the project checks locally before pushing:

    just test          # schema generation, Python datamodels, pytest, schema lint
just lint          # LinkML schema lint
just docs-strict   # build docs in strict mode

  4. Update the docs alongside the schema. Changes to src/astra/schema/*.yaml should also touch docs/specification.md and the relevant tables. The auto-generated field reference is regenerated by just gen-doc.

items.title: Adding schema elements
items.text:
Schema changes follow a small ritual:

# Edit src/astra/schema/{types,analysis,insight,provenance}.yaml
# For a rule: its row in its section's codes table in docs/specification.md, and,
# for a schema-layer rule, its code on the constraint (annotations: {rule: CODE})

just gen-schema    # Regenerate the contract in project/ (commit it)
just gen-python    # Regenerate Python datamodels
just gen-doc       # Regenerate the field reference docs (docs/elements/)
just lint          # Lint the LinkML schema
just test          # Run all tests

Open a PR with the schema, generated artefacts, and any doc updates in a single commit so reviewers see the full picture. Every schema constraint needs a row in NEGATIVE (tests/test_constraints.py), and a new schema-layer code an invalid fixture in tests/data/invalid/.

items.title: Reporting problems
items.text:
A useful issue includes:

  • The version of astra-spec and astra-tools (run astra --version and astra schema show analysis | head -2).
  • A minimal astra.yaml that reproduces the problem.
  • The full error output, copy-pasted from the terminal.
  • What you expected to happen instead.

Validation issues are easier to triage when accompanied by a fixture small enough to drop into tests/data/ — usually a single decision and a single output is plenty.

items.title: Code of Conduct
items.text: We expect respectful, thoughtful collaboration in all project spaces — issues, pull requests, and discussions. Treat other contributors the way you would want to be treated; assume good faith; disagree with the idea, not the person. Conduct issues can be raised privately with the maintainers via GitHub.

items.title: Citing and license
items.text: For citation guidance and license details, see the About page.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
A self-contained tour of the ASTRA format: scaffold a project, edit the analysis, validate it, inspect it, define universes, and attach evidence. It assumes the astra CLI is already installed — see installation.

If you'd rather see the schema first, jump to the specification.

items.title: Scaffold a project
items.text:
Use astra init to create a minimal project layout:

astra init my-analysis
cd my-analysis

This produces:

my-analysis/
└── astra.yaml              # Analysis specification (source of truth)

The scaffolded astra.yaml is a complete, valid analysis: a spec_version and one output, result, a JSON metric made by python src/result.py '{output}'. It validates as-is — you can edit incrementally rather than rewriting from scratch.

Tip: Where no git repository holds the new directory, astra init runs git init in it. It makes no commit.

astra init never overwrites existing files, so it is safe to run in a directory that already has content; where the directory already has an astra.yaml, it stops with an error and leaves it untouched.

items.title: Edit the analysis
items.text:
The scaffold gives you a working starting point; what follows is a boiled-down view of the structure you'll be editing. Every analysis states its spec_version and usually declares its outputs:, with inputs: and decisions: — plus optional metadata (label, description, tags).

spec_version: "0.1.0"
label: My Analysis

description: |                    # short free-prose orientation
  One paragraph describing the analysis.

inputs:
  primary_data:
    path: data/primary.csv        # a file tracked in git with the analysis
    description: "Source dataset"

outputs:
  main_result:
    type: metric                  # metric | figure | table | data | report
    format: json                  # file extension, no dot; required from 0.1.0
    description: "Primary output"
    decisions: [example_method]   # contract: only these decisions are visible to the recipe
    recipe:
      command: python src/main.py --method {decisions.example_method} --out {output}

decisions:
  example_method:
    label: "Example Method"
    options:
      option_a: { label: "Option A" }
      option_b: { label: "Option B" }

A few things worth noting:

  • Decisions parameterize outputs. Output.decisions declares the contract — only the listed decisions resolve inside recipe.command. The validator rejects {decisions.foo} if foo isn't in the list.
  • Recipe placeholders. Four forms are legal: {inputs} (all declared inputs, space-separated), {inputs.<id>} (one declared input), {decisions.<id>} (one declared decision), and {output} (where to write). {{ and }} are literal braces.
  • Rich reports live alongside astra.yaml. The spec keeps a single optional description; a fuller write-up — figures, citations, multi-page structure — is built next to the analysis and references its elements rather than restating them. MySTRA is one framework that does this.
  • Constraints between options. requires: and incompatible_with: (format: decision.option) gate which option combinations are valid. They are checked against each universe when you validate the analysis.

items.title: Validate
items.text:
Run astra validate on the analysis's folder:

astra validate .

Validation runs in three stages, each gating the next:

  1. Parsing — the file is YAML 1.2 whose content is a map, with no key twice.
  2. Schema validation — the JSON Schema (generated from the LinkML schema) checks types, required fields, and format patterns (ID pattern, version pattern, DOI pattern, …).
  3. Semantic validation — clashing IDs, input files exist and are tracked in git, declared analyses and addresses resolve, recipe template placeholders match Output.inputs / Output.decisions, output dependency graph has no cycles, constraint references resolve, universes are complete and consistent.

A clean run prints:

astra.yaml: valid, 0 error(s), 0 warning(s)

When something is wrong, errors print by file, as line:col level CODE message:

astra.yaml
  20:16 error UNDECLARED_TEMPLATE_REF `{decisions.foo}` isn't a placeholder of this output: it takes `{inputs}`, `{output}`, and `{inputs.<entry>}` and `{decisions.<entry>}` for an entry of its `inputs` or `decisions` as written; `{{` and `}}` are literal braces
astra.yaml: invalid, 1 error(s), 0 warning(s)

Non-blocking warnings print in yellow: the validator still returns success but surfaces them so authors can clean the record up.

items.title: Inspect
items.text:
astra info prints a Rich-rendered summary: the analysis label, and its declarations, inputs, outputs, decisions and universes, followed by the same for each analysis it declares, if any.

astra info

astra.yaml  My Analysis
  inputs    primary_data: data/primary.csv
  outputs   main_result: metric, json
  decisions example_method: option_a, option_b

Once the analysis has universes (next section), astra universe list and astra universe show name them and give each one's selection, and astra plan lists the results they plan, with where each goes and its command.

items.title: Define universes
items.text:
A universe is one complete set of decision selections — one option per decision it uses, of the analysis and of the analyses it drives. Each universe yields one set of results; the same analysis can carry many of them.

Universes are written in astra.yaml, under universes:: there is no default universe or option (Elements).

universes:
  baseline:
    description: Default configuration using standard practices
    decisions:
      example_method: option_a

Add a second universe by hand, next to baseline, to flex an alternative path:

universes:
  alt:
    description: Alternative method choice
    decisions:
      example_method: option_b

Validate, and inspect the universes:

astra validate .              # full validation, universes included
astra universe show alt       # the selection alt makes
astra plan                    # the planned results and their commands

Universe validation enforces three rules, among others: every decision the universe uses, of the analysis and of the analyses it drives, has a selection; each selection names an option that exists on its decision; and no requires: / incompatible_with: constraint among the decisions it uses is violated. If the analysis says model.svm requires scaling.standard, a universe selecting svm must also select standard — the validator points to the offending pair.

For declared analyses, the universe sets their decisions by address (Elements):

analyses:
  feature_extraction:
    path: feature_extraction
universes:
  baseline:
    decisions:
      random_seed: seed_42              # root decision
      feature_extraction.method: pca    # selection inside a sub-analysis

items.title: Add evidence (optional)
items.text:
ASTRA decisions can cite literature. You author the citation in astra.yaml — a prior_insight with a claim, the source DOI, and the quoted text that supports it — and link the insight to the decision option it justifies:

prior_insights:
  attention_scales:
    claim: "Self-attention scales better than recurrence."
    evidence:
      - doi: "10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762"
        version: 7
        quote:
          exact: "Attention Is All You Need"

decisions:
  architecture:
    label: "Architecture"
    options:
      transformer:
        label: "Transformer"
        insights: [attention_scales]   # link the option to the insight
      rnn:
        label: "RNN"

The chain option → insight → evidence → DOI is what gives a decision an auditable trail back to the literature.

astra paper verify reads each evidence entry that cites a DOI, looks up the cached PDF for that DOI, and fuzzy-matches the quote.exact against the extracted text:

astra paper verify .

Papers are kept in a cache under ~/.cache/astra/papers/. astra paper add puts one there, and astra paper list shows which cited papers the cache holds. A paper missing from the cache, or a quote not found, is a warning, never an error.

Artifact-backed evidence (typical for findings:) cites an output's results rather than a paper: astra paper verify leaves it alone, and astra check gives it the status of the results it cites.

items.title: What ASTRA doesn't run
items.text:
The CLI validates and inspects analyses, and checks results against their records; it does not execute recipes. Each recipe.command is a POSIX shell command that a runner — an agent, a workflow runner, a notebook, or you on the command line — reads and invokes (Results). The runner materialises the declared inputs (giving each one a concrete on-disk path), picks an output path, expands the {inputs.<id>} / {inputs} / {decisions.<id>} / {output} placeholders against the universe being built, runs the resulting command, and writes the result with a record of the run, which astra check later compares with the analysis.

This separation is intentional: the spec stays stable as the agent and execution layer evolves. ASTRA's job is to make every analytical choice explicit, traceable, and verifiable; the choice of runner is yours.

items.title: Governance
items.text:
ASTRA is developed in the open and is intended to evolve towards a community-owned standard. This page documents who makes decisions today, how those decisions are made, and how that structure is expected to evolve. It is the companion to the RFC process, which is the mechanism through which most decisions are actually made and recorded.

Draft governance — alpha

ASTRA is in alpha. This page describes the governance model as a full-featured draft: the structure below is what the project commits to at v0.1. Until then, ASTRA is stewarded by Lightcone Research, and decisions rest with the Lightcone Research core team, with all discussion in public issues and pull requests. There is no formal voting process during alpha — the RFC acceptance bar becomes binding at v0.1.

items.title: Stewardship
items.text: ASTRA is currently stewarded by Lightcone Research, which writes most of the code and documentation today. This stewardship is a starting point, not the long-term home: as ASTRA stabilizes beyond alpha, the project will move into a community-governed structure.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Steering Council. Provides high-level technical and strategic direction, safeguards the project's principles, oversees the RFC process, and acts as final approver for RFCs. During alpha this role is held by the Lightcone Research core team; it is expected to expand at v0.1 into a dedicated council as outside contributors join, drawing on the models used by the Python Software Foundation and Project Jupyter.

Maintainers. Actively design, implement, and maintain the schema, tooling, and documentation; review and approve pull requests. Maintainer status emerges through sustained contribution rather than appointment, and may span organizations and tool ecosystems.

Contributors and community. Anyone may open an issue, propose an RFC, or submit code and documentation, provided they follow the Code of Conduct. The governance structure exists to enable progress and stewardship — not to restrict contribution. In alpha, the most valuable contributions are real-analysis attempts, adversarial schema review, and downstream tooling experiments; see the Community page.

items.title: How decisions are made
items.text: Significant or contested changes go through the RFC process. Decisions and their rationale are recorded durably as accepted (and rejected) RFCs, so the project's evolution stays auditable.

items.title: Code of Conduct
items.text: All participation in ASTRA's spaces — issues, pull requests, and discussions — is governed by the organization-wide Contributor Covenant 3.0 Code of Conduct. Conduct concerns can be raised privately with the project leads at the addresses listed there. Treat other contributors the way you would want to be treated; assume good faith; disagree with the idea, not the person.

items.title: Changing this document
items.text: Governance and process changes are themselves made by RFC. The procedural baseline was established in RFC 0001; amendments — including the composition of the Steering Council and the exact acceptance thresholds — follow the same path.

items.title: Installation
items.text: astra comes in the astra-tools package. It needs Python 3.11 or later and git, which it runs to read repositories.

items.title: Install
items.text:
With uv, which keeps astra apart from your projects' environments:

uv tool install astra-tools

With pip:

pip install astra-tools

While astra-tools for ASTRA 0.1 has only release candidates, uv and pip skip them. Ask for them with uv tool install --prerelease allow astra-tools, or pip install --pre astra-tools.

To run it once without installing it, name the version:

uvx astra-tools@<version> validate

Check that it works:

astra --version
astra --help

items.title: Which ASTRA it reads
items.text:
astra-tools reads ASTRA 0.1 files, those whose spec_version is 0.1.x. It installs the schemas and rules of the specification with it, as the astra-spec package. A file written for ASTRA 0.0.x states its version as version:, and fails the schema checks: MISSING_FIELD for spec_version, UNKNOWN_FIELD for version, and others. The 0.2 line of astra-tools reads such a file as it is:

uv tool install 'astra-tools<0.3'

  • Tab completion for bash, zsh and fish is one line in your shell's startup file.

items.title: RFC process
items.text:
The Request for Comments (RFC) process is how significant changes to ASTRA are proposed, discussed, and decided in the open. It exists to keep major decisions transparent, to invite participation without requiring deep prior context, and to leave a durable, citable record of what changed and why — the same values ASTRA asks of the analyses it describes.

Draft process — alpha

ASTRA is in alpha, and this process is published as a full-featured draft. Until ASTRA reaches v0.1, decisions rest with the Lightcone Research core team, with all discussion in public issues and pull requests. The time-boxed review window and multi-approver acceptance bar described below become binding at v0.1, when the Steering Council expands beyond the core team. See Governance.

The process is modeled on MyST Enhancement Proposals, and the PEP/Jupyter lineage behind it.

items.title: When you need an RFC
items.text:
You do not need an RFC for low-risk changes — typo and documentation fixes, tightened error messages, an obviously-missing enum value. Open an issue or a pull request directly.

You do want an RFC when a change is significant, contested, or worth recording the rationale for:

  • new schema concepts or breaking changes to existing ones,
  • versioning and compatibility rules,
  • publishing, identifier, and metadata conventions,
  • changes to the process or governance itself.

items.title: What an RFC is — and is not
items.text: An ASTRA RFC is a written proposal for a significant change, scoped narrowly enough to review and implement in a reasonable timeframe, and grounded in real or anticipated use. It is not a full system design, a comprehensive ontology, a guarantee of permanence, or a substitute for implementation. RFCs are working agreements that may be revised or superseded as ASTRA matures.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
RFCs live in the rfcs/ directory of the astra-spec repository, as numbered Markdown files. The process leans on GitHub's native pull-request signals rather than a custom set of labels: a draft PR means the RFC is being worked on; marking it ready for review opens the decision window. Each RFC's own status: frontmatter field is the durable record of where it ended up.

  1. Open an issue. Describe the idea using the RFC proposal issue template (which carries the rfc label), so others can react and you get an early signal before investing in a full draft.
  2. Open a draft pull request. Add rfcs/NNNN-short-slug.md, copied from 0000-template.md, with status: Draft, and open the PR as a GitHub draft. The template's sections are Context · Proposal · Examples · Implementation implications & migration · Questions or objections · References.
  3. Discuss and iterate. While the PR is a draft, invite discussion, incorporate feedback, and record objections and their responses in the RFC. Treat revisions as success, not failure.
  4. Open the decision window. When the proposal has stabilized and the author wants to move forward, mark the PR ready for review and set the RFC to status: Active. The ready-for-review timestamp starts the review clock.
  5. Decide. The RFC is Accepted or Rejected, recorded by setting status: accordingly in the frontmatter. Both outcomes are merged: an accepted RFC records the agreement, a rejected RFC records the reasoning so the question is not silently re-litigated. An author may instead close the PR to withdraw a proposal.
  6. Implement. Accepted RFCs move into implementation following the project's normal development practices (schema change + regenerated artifacts + docs in one reviewed pull request).

items.title: Statuses
items.text:
A status lives in each RFC's status: frontmatter field; the table below maps it to the corresponding pull-request state, so the two never need separate labels to stay in sync.

status: Meaning Pull-request state Draft Under active drafting and discussion; not yet up for a decision. Draft PR Active Stabilized; in the open review window. Ready for review Accepted Approved. Implementation may begin (or has begun). Merged Rejected Declined, but merged for the record with the rationale intact. Merged Superseded Replaced by a later RFC (recorded in its superseded-by field). (set later)

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
Becomes binding at v0.1

During alpha, the Lightcone Research core team accepts or rejects an RFC after open discussion; there is no fixed quorum. From v0.1, an RFC may be accepted when all of the following hold:

  • it has been Active for a minimum open review window (proposed: at least five weekdays),
  • it has the required Steering Council approvals (proposed: at least two), and
  • there are no outstanding requests for changes from a Steering Council member.

If a blocking objection is raised, the author may revise and restart the decision once the objection is addressed. The exact numbers are themselves subject to refinement by RFC as the Steering Council grows.

items.title: Relationship to versioning
items.text: When an accepted RFC changes the schema, its Implementation implications & migration section should state whether the change is a minor or major bump under ASTRA's versioning policy and what migration (if any) existing analyses need. The mechanics of versioned schema hosting — per-version docs and machine-fetchable schemas at stable URLs — are already in place; see the About page and the canonical https://w3id.org/astra/ namespace.

items.title: The ASTRA specification
items.text: ASTRA records a research analysis, a folder in a git repository with an astra.yaml at its top, so that every choice in it is explicit and every result can be checked against how it was made. Analyses communicate natively, sharing inputs, outputs and decisions by address. A validator checks the files against git, a runner builds the results from committed files and writes a record of how each was made, and a checker later compares each record with the analysis as it then is.

items.title: Elements
items.text:
An astra.yaml (YAML 1.2) gives its spec_version ("0.1.0") and maps of elements, each keyed by its id ([a-z][a-z0-9_]*). The snippets below are parts of analysis/astra.yaml, the file of the analysis in the folder analysis/, and its paths are relative.

  • An analysis can declare other analyses:
# analysis/astra.yaml
analyses:
  stage: {path: stage}
  previous: {path: ., commit: <commit id>}
  module: {path: module, commit: <commit id>}
  upstream: {url: <url of a git repository>, commit: <commit id>}
  • stage: the folder analysis/stage/, read from the working tree, which, once committed, lets it be built
  • previous: analysis/ itself at a commit
  • module: a git submodule at analysis/module/, as analysis's repository holds it at that commit
  • upstream: a remote repository at a commit

Elements of a declared analysis are obtained by address (declarations followed by an element, joined by dots): stage.output3 points to output3 defined in stage.

The folder at its commit, or in the working tree, is the analysis's identity: one folder at one commit is one analysis however it is declared, and another analysis is one with another identity.

  • An input is one file, tracked in git with its analysis, at a path from the analysis's folder; a stand-in, such as a large-file pointer, may take its place where a tool recognises it.
inputs:
  input1: {path: data/input1.csv}

The path stays inside the analysis's folder, outside results/, .astra/ and any folder contained within the analysis's folder with its own astra.yaml. Another analysis's input is read by address in an output (stage.input2); other data, such as a download, comes in as an output whose recipe gets it.

  • A decision lists the options of a scientific choice. An option may be excluded with a reason, cite prior insights, and carry constraints: options it requires or is incompatible_with, by option reference, a decision's address then an option's id (decision1.b, stage.decision2.b).
decisions:
  decision1:
    rationale: Both are reasonable, and they may give different results.
    options:
      a:
        insights: [insight2]
      b:
        requires: [stage.decision2.b]
      c:
        excluded: It needs data this analysis doesn't have.
  • insight2 supports option a
  • b requires stage's decision2 to be b

  • c is excluded and never selected

  • An output, unless it is a switch (below), has a type, a format (its file extension), the decisions it is made with, what it reads (inputs, ordered), and a recipe: a POSIX shell command, run in its analysis's folder, whose placeholders {inputs}, {inputs.<entry>}, {decisions.<entry>} and {output} become paths and selected options, verbatim. Its result is the one file the recipe writes.

outputs:
  output1:
    type: metric
    format: json
    inputs: [input1, stage.output3, upstream.output4]
    decisions: [decision1, stage.decision2]
    recipe:
      command: python src/output1.py {inputs} {decisions.decision1} {decisions.stage.decision2} {output}

Another analysis's elements are read by address in an output's inputs, decisions, switch and cases, a constraint or evidence, just as if they were the analysis's own: output1 reads stage's output3 and is made with stage's decision2, whatever option is selected where it is built.

  • A switch is an output with a switch, a decision's address, and cases, from options of that decision to references; it has no type, format, inputs, decisions or recipe, and no result, record, name or place of its own. In each universe it takes the case of the option its decision selects there, and reading it reads what that case names.
outputs:
  switch1:
    switch: decision1
    cases:
      b: stage.output3
  output6:
    type: figure
    format: png
    inputs: [switch1]
    decisions: [decision3]
    recipe:
      command: python src/output6.py {inputs.switch1} {decisions.decision3} {output}
decisions:
  decision3:
    options: {a: {}, b: {}}
  • where decision1 selects b, switch1 takes stage.output3, and {inputs.switch1} is the path of its result there
  • a has no case: where decision1 selects a, switch1 isn't built (below), nor is output6, which reads it without a pin, and nothing there uses decision3
  • a case names an input, an output or a switch, of the analysis or by address; options may share a case; and a case may name an excluded option, such as decision1's c, and is then never taken

  • a case that names a switch nests the two; by convention, the switch on the decision that decides whether the other matters is the outer one

  • A universe selects an option for each decision it uses (below): its own analysis's by id, another's by address. With derived_from it inherits another universe's selection, replacing what it sets: its effective selection. Its own decisions set only decisions it uses on some branch, and should set only those it uses.

universes:
  u1:
    decisions:
      decision1: b
      decision3: a
      stage.decision2: b
  u2:
    derived_from: u1
    decisions: {decision1: a}
  • u1 sets stage's decision2: it drives stage (below)

  • u2 changes decision1 from u1's b to a, and keeps stage.decision2 as b and decision3 as a, which it doesn't use: output6 isn't built there

  • An entry of an output's inputs, or a switch's case, is a reference: an address that may end in a pin, # and a universe's id, fixing the universe it reads. #u names, in order:

  • the universes entry u in the same astra.yaml as the pin;
  • else the universe u of the declared analysis whose element the reference names;
  • else nothing, which breaks UNKNOWN_PIN_UNIVERSE.
outputs:
  output2:
    type: table
    format: csv
    inputs: [output1#u1, output1#u2, stage.output3#v1]
    recipe:
      command: python src/output2.py {inputs} {output}
  • output2 reads output1 as built in u1 and in u2
  • analysis has no v1, so stage.output3#v1 reads stage's own result in its v1

  • a pinned switch reads as it is in its pin's universe: switch1#u1 reads stage.output3 as built in u1

  • An output other than a switch is built per universe if it lists decisions, or reads without a pin a switch or an output built per universe; it has a result in each universe where it and its analysis are built (below). Otherwise it is built once, with one result:

outputs:
  output1:
    decisions: [decision1, stage.decision2]
    ...
  output2:
    inputs: [output1#u1, output1#u2]
    ...
- output1 is built per universe because it lists decisions - output2 is built once because it only reads output1 pinned to specific universes - output6 is built per universe because it lists decision3; reading switch1 without a pin would be reason enough

Were it also to have:

outputs:
  output7:
    inputs: [output1]
    ...
- output7 is built per universe because it reads output1, which is built per universe, without a pin

  • The analysis being validated or built, here analysis, is the driving analysis. Its universes can set the decisions of the analyses it declares, and of those they declare in turn; where they do, it drives them:
universes:
  u1:
    decisions:
      ...
      stage.decision2: b

In u1, stage is built with decision2: b, whatever its own universes say. The stage.output3 that output1 reads is built with b selected for stage.decision2, and its result belongs to analysis.

A universe sets a decision further down by its full address. Were stage to declare inner, which has a decision4, and output1 to list it as stage.inner.decision4:

universes:
  u1:
    decisions:
      ...
      stage.decision2: b
      stage.inner.decision4: a
  u2:
    derived_from: u1
    decisions: {decision1: a}
- stage.inner.decision4 drives stage and drives inner through stage

The analyses an address goes through, here stage then inner, form a chain. Once any universe drives a chain, every universe must set the decisions of the analyses on it that it uses: had u2 not derived from u1, it would have to set stage.decision2 and stage.inner.decision4 itself, as output1 lists both.

  • Each chain is driven on its own. Were analysis/astra.yaml also to declare inner directly, and set none of its decisions:

    analyses:
  inner: {path: stage/inner}
outputs:
  output11:
    inputs: [inner.output8]
    ...

    this chain isn't driven, even though stage.inner is. Through it, output11 can read inner's outputs built once, or pinned to inner's own universes, but not one built per universe in u1 or u2.

  • An analysis with no decisions of its own, or none that a universe of the driving analysis uses, has nothing to set. Were analysis/astra.yaml also to declare tools, which has none:

    # analysis/tools/astra.yaml
analyses:
  parent: {path: ..}
inputs:
  input3: {path: data/input3.csv}
outputs:
  output9:
    inputs: [input3]
    ...
  output10:
    decisions: [parent.decision1]
    ...
    • tools.output9 just exists as tools's result
    • tools.output10 varies, so it is built in u1 and u2, and those results belong to analysis
    • were tools to have a decision that only output9 lists, it would still have nothing to set, as analysis reads nothing of output9

  • An analysis never drives itself. A universe can't set a decision through a declaration that leads back, such as self: {path: .}, or stage's parent: {path: ..}. Writing self.decision1: b instead of decision1: b would break LOOPING_KEY:

    universes:
  u1:
    decisions:
      decision1: b       # self.decision1: b would break LOOPING_KEY

  • stage's own universes, such as v1, don't set its decisions in u1 and u2, but must still be valid, with stage as the driving analysis: a v1 that left decision2 unset would break MISSING_DECISION, as stage plans output3, which lists it. A pin into v1 can then read only what uses decisions that v1 uses on some branch, as v1 may set no other.

  • An output that reads another analysis's output built per universe, or its switch, without a pin or pinned to one of its own analysis's universes (stage.output3#u1), or uses one of its decisions, needs that analysis driven: an output uses the decisions it lists, and a switch the decision it switches on; a switch reads only the case it takes. output1 reads stage.output3 and uses stage.decision2, so were no universe of analysis to set a decision of stage:

    universes:
  u1:
    decisions: {decision1: b}   # nothing of stage's: stage isn't driven

    output1 would break NOT_BUILT_IN_UNIVERSE: nothing would say which decision2 to build stage.output3 with. It could still read what doesn't vary: stage.input2, stage.output3#v1, or upstream.output4, which is built once.

  • A switch can choose between analyses. Were analysis/astra.yaml also to declare fast and slow, each with an output fit that lists a decision5 of its own:

    outputs:
  switch2:
    switch: decision1
    cases: {a: fast.fit, b: slow.fit}

    a universe where decision1 selects a would use, and set, fast.decision5 and nothing of slow's, and one where it selects b the reverse.

By convention, a decision that matters to one analysis is driven, and one shared by several, such as a seed, is read by address from the analysis that holds it.

  • Were stage to have a u1 of its own, #u1 in analysis/astra.yaml would still name analysis's. To read stage's own u1 too it must be imported under another id and pinned to that. An import selects and drives nothing.
universes:
  stage_u1: {analysis: stage, universe: u1}
outputs:
  output5:
    type: table
    format: csv
    inputs:
      - stage.output3#u1
      - stage.output3#stage_u1
    recipe:
      command: python src/output5.py {inputs} {output}
  • stage.output3#u1 is built in, and belongs to, analysis's u1

  • stage.output3#stage_u1 is built in stage's own u1 and belongs to stage

  • An insight is a claim whose evidence cites a doi or an output (artifact): prior_insights are what the analysis builds on, findings what it concludes. An artifact is a reference, like an output's inputs entry: it may be pinned, by address it reads another analysis's output, and it may name a switch each of whose cases names an output other than a switch, or a switch like it.

prior_insights:
  insight2:
    claim: An earlier study found that decision1 changes the result.
    evidence:
      - doi: 10.5555/12345678
        location: {value: page=6}
findings:
  insight1:
    claim: The two universes give different results.
    evidence:
      - artifact: output2

items.title: Results
items.text:
• A result is the one file an output's recipe writes: an output built once has one, and an output built per universe has one in each universe where it is built and its analysis is built. An output other than a switch is built in a universe if everything it reads there without a pin is an input, an output built once, or built there; a switch is built there if its decision selects there an option with a case that names one of these or, pinned, something built in its pin's universe. Whether an output is built never depends on driving.

  • The driving analysis plans from its own outputs other than switches that no case of its own names, its own switches that no inputs entry or case of its own names, and what its evidence cites. It plans their results where they are built, a switch's being those of the case it takes, and every result a planned result reads, through any declaration and the case each switch takes; nothing else is made. An output that a case names is so planned, as another analysis's is, only where something planned reads it: one that is also a deliverable must be read or cited elsewhere to be built where that case isn't taken.

  • were switch1's case for b an output of analysis's own, that output would be planned only because output6 reads it in u1, not for itself

  • The driving analysis reaches what it plans from, built or not: an output built once, and evidence citing one, once; other pinned evidence in its pin's universe; anything else in each of its universes. It reaches too whatever something reached reads, there or, pinned, in its pin's universe: each entry of an output, and only the case a switch takes.

  • in u2, output6 is reached, and so is switch1, which takes no case there

  • A universe uses, with its own analysis as the driving analysis, each decision that a result planned in it lists or a switch reached in it switches on.

  • u1 uses decision1, decision3 and stage.decision2; u2 uses decision1 and stage.decision2, but not decision3, as output6 isn't built there

  • A universe uses on some branch each decision listed or switched on by what its analysis would reach in it were every case of every switch followed. So that a universe can set a key only for those derived from it, it also uses on some branch each decision that a universe inheriting its key for it, without setting it, uses on some branch.

  • u2 uses decision3 on some branch, as output6, which lists it, is reached there

  • In a universe, the decisions in play are those it uses and, in a universe of an analysis other than the driving analysis, those that something reached through a pin uses there. Constraints are judged among them: a decision not in play counts as selecting nothing.

  • A result belongs to the analysis whose universe built it or, for an output built once, the analysis whose output it is. With stage's own file:

# analysis/stage/astra.yaml
spec_version: "0.1.0"
inputs:
  input2: {path: data/input2.csv}
decisions:
  decision2:
    options: {a: {}, b: {}}
outputs:
  output3:
    type: data
    format: csv
    inputs: [input2]
    decisions: [decision2]
    recipe:
      command: python src/output3.py {inputs.input2} {decisions.decision2} {output}
universes:
  v1:
    decisions: {decision2: a}

the build is:

┌─ u1 · analysis's own ────────────────────────────────┐
│  input1 ────────────────────────┐                    │
│  stage.output3 (decision2 = b) ─┼─► output1          │── #u1 ──┐
│  upstream.output4 ──────────────┘   (decision1 = b)  │         │
│  stage.output3 ─► switch1 (b) ────► output6          │         │
│                                     (decision3 = a)  │         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
┌─ u2 · analysis's own ────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  input1 ────────────────────────┐                    │         ▼
│  stage.output3 (decision2 = b) ─┼─► output1          │── #u2 ──► output2 ◄── insight1
│  upstream.output4 ──────────────┘   (decision1 = a)  │         ▲
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
┌─ v1 · stage's own ───────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  output3 (decision2 = a)                             │── #v1 ──┘
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  • the planned results are output2, output1 in u1 and u2, output6 in u1, stage.output3 in u1, u2 and v1, and upstream.output4; output6 isn't built in u2, where switch1 has no case for a

  • A runner builds each planned result by running its output's recipe in a checkout of a commit, with no changes but records and results, and writes the result's bytes and a record of how it was made. Results of an analysis declared with a commit, and of the analyses it declares, directly or not, are results from a commit: never rebuilt, but read through their records, and their bytes (or a stand-in), at their analysis's commit. Driven, such an analysis runs its recipes on exactly its files at its commit. A switch of such an analysis is read with its files at its commit: the result its case gives is a result from a commit or, where the analysis is driven, one built on its files at that commit.

  • at its commit, upstream has an output output4, built once, with its result and record committed: the runner reads them and runs no recipe of upstream's

  • previous reads the analysis's own earlier results the same way

  • A record holds what its commit can't give: the result's address, content hash and size and, under generated_by, the commit it was made from, the hash and size of each input by its entry, the environment it ran in and the runner. The record of output1 in u1:

{
  "spec_version": "0.1.0",
  "address": "output1#u1",
  "content_hash": "sha256:<hash>",
  "size": <size>,
  "generated_by": {
    "commit": "<commit id>",
    "inputs": [
      {"entry": "input1", "content_hash": "sha256:<hash>", "size": <size>},
      {"entry": "stage.output3", "content_hash": "sha256:<hash>", "size": <size>},
      {"entry": "upstream.output4", "content_hash": "sha256:<hash>", "size": <size>}
    ],
    "environment": {"iri": "urn:example:environment1"},
    "runner": {"id": "example-runner", "version": "1.0.0"}
  }
}
  • A checker later compares each record with the analysis as it then is, and gives each planned result a record status:
  • missing if there is no record, or one that doesn't parse or meet its schema, names another address, or doesn't list exactly the inputs its output had at the record's commit;
  • else stale if anything it is made from has changed since the record's commit;

  • else unchanged.

  • A result is made from its output's command, inputs in order, decisions and format; the options those decisions select in its universe; for each switch it reads through, the decision it switches on, the option selected for it where it is read and the case it takes; its inputs' content, never a stand-in's; and the results it reads. Code (fixed by the commit) and the environment (installed software, container) are recorded, not compared: an edited script shows only once a rerun makes other bytes. A result made from a stale or missing one is stale until that one is rebuilt with the hash it recorded. A record otherwise in order leaves its result stale if its commit can't be read (squashed or rebased away) or its output is gone at that commit, where MISSING_RECORD_INPUTS isn't judged, or if an input is behind a stand-in that gives no hash. In the example:

Edit Effect analysis/stage/data/input2.csv changes The seven results built are stale; upstream.output4 stays unchanged u2 selects a for stage.decision2 stage.output3 and output1 in u2 are stale, and so is output2, which reads output1#u2 switch1's case for b becomes upstream.output4 output6 in u1 is stale insight1's claim is reworded Every result stays unchanged analysis/src/output1.py is edited Every result stays unchanged; once output1 is rebuilt with other bytes, output2 is stale

  • A result's bytes are present if its default place (below) holds the recorded ones, else absent. The record of a result from a commit, at the declared commit B, names an earlier commit A; the result is unchanged if nothing compared changed between A and B and the results it was made from are unchanged, and gets a bytes status, from what B holds, only if a recipe reads it.

  • Evidence takes the status of the result it cites. Citing without a pin an output built per universe, or a switch, it cites that output's results in the driving analysis's universes or, for a switch, the result in each of them of the case it takes there: none means missing, several the worst status. A check covers a declared analysis's evidence only where it cites a planned result.

  • A result's name is its output's id after the driven declarations leading there from the analysis it belongs to (stage.output3); two driven chains give two names. Its address adds # and its universe's own id (stage.output3#u1). Each name gives the result, in the folder of the analysis it belongs to, a place for its record, .astra/records/{universe}/{name}.json, and a default place for its bytes, results/{universe}/{name}.{format}; built once, neither has {universe}/. A switch has no name or place: a result read through one keeps its own. The build above leaves:

analysis/.astra/records/output2.json             analysis/results/output2.csv
analysis/.astra/records/u1/output1.json          analysis/results/u1/output1.json
analysis/.astra/records/u1/output6.json          analysis/results/u1/output6.png
analysis/.astra/records/u1/stage.output3.json    analysis/results/u1/stage.output3.csv
analysis/.astra/records/u2/output1.json          analysis/results/u2/output1.json
analysis/.astra/records/u2/stage.output3.json    analysis/results/u2/stage.output3.csv
analysis/stage/.astra/records/v1/output3.json    analysis/stage/results/v1/output3.csv

items.title: Rules
items.text:
Each rule has a code, a level (MUST or SHOULD, as in BCP 14) and a layer, set by what its tool sees: one file (parse, schema), the stack's files and git (validator), also records and results (check), or its own runs (runner). The driving analysis's stack is it and every analysis it declares, directly or not. In the first four layers a broken MUST is an error and a broken SHOULD a warning; a runner that breaks a MUST doesn't conform. A file is valid if it breaks no parse or schema rule, read by the schema of its spec_version's minor version (0.1 for 0.1.2); an analysis is valid if no analysis of its stack breaks a MUST of the first three layers. A broken check rule gives the status after the arrow. Rows that share a code are cases of one rule.

Code Level Rule parse INVALID_SYNTAX MUST An astra.yaml is a YAML 1.2 document holding a map INVALID_SYNTAX MUST A record is UTF-8 JSON text, no object repeating a name schema MISSING_FIELD MUST astra.yaml has spec_version; an output other than a switch, type, format and recipe.command MISSING_FIELD MUST An input has path; a decision, options; an insight, claim, evidence; quote, exact; location, value MISSING_FIELD MUST A record has every field but started, finished and inputs UNKNOWN_FIELD MUST Every field is one the schema defines WRONG_TYPE MUST Every value has its field's JSON type, never null (leave an optional field out) EMPTY_COLLECTION MUST options, cases, evidence and every list of strings in astra.yaml are non-empty DUPLICATE_ENTRY MUST No list of strings holds one entry twice INVALID_VALUE MUST type is metric, figure, table, data or report; format matches ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.+-]*$ INVALID_VALUE MUST Every spec_version, hash, IRI, time, doi, url and location value has its form INVALID_VALUE MUST size ≥ 0, evidence version ≥ 1, resources.cpus ≥ 0, resources.gpus ≥ 1 INVALID_ID MUST Map keys and id-typed values are ids; a universe's decisions keys are addresses INVALID_REFERENCE MUST Every address, reference and option reference, bar universe keys, matches its grammar INVALID_PATH MUST Every input's and declaration's path is non-empty and doesn't start with / INVALID_IMPORT MUST A universes entry with analysis or universe has both, and no decisions or derived_from INVALID_SWITCH MUST An outputs entry with switch or cases has both, and no type, format, inputs, decisions or recipe INVALID_EVIDENCE_SOURCE MUST Evidence has exactly one of doi and artifact, and version only with doi INVALID_DECLARATION_SOURCE MUST A declaration has exactly one of path and url URL_WITHOUT_COMMIT MUST A declaration with a url has a commit INVALID_COMMIT MUST Every commit is a full commit id: 40 or 64 lowercase hex digits validator NOT_IN_REPOSITORY MUST The driving analysis is in a git repository's working tree MISSING_INPUT_FILE MUST An input's path names a file (no symlink, folder or gitlink) or a stand-in INPUT_NOT_TRACKED MUST An input's file or stand-in is tracked in its analysis's repository INPUT_IN_ANOTHER_ANALYSIS MUST An input's file is in its analysis's folder, in no nested analysis (a folder below with an astra.yaml) RESERVED_PATH MUST No input or declaration path is, or lies inside, a stack analysis's results/ or .astra/ in its tree MISSING_DECLARED_ANALYSIS MUST A declared folder holds an astra.yaml, reached through no symlink DECLARATION_OUTSIDE_REPOSITORY MUST A tidied declaration path doesn't go above the top of the driving analysis's working tree or, at a commit, of its repository COMMIT_NOT_FOUND MUST In a file not read from a remote, a path and commit name a commit of the file's repository DECLARED_ANALYSIS_INVALID MUST An analysis from a commit, with all it declares, is valid at that commit UNRESOLVED_ADDRESS MUST An address in inputs or cases names an input or output; in artifact, an output other than a switch, or a switch each of whose cases names one of these UNRESOLVED_ADDRESS MUST In decisions, switch, universe keys and option references, a decision; in an import, another analysis's universe AMBIGUOUS_ID MUST No input and output of one analysis share an id CLASHING_RESULT_NAME MUST No output shares its id with a declaration of its analysis UNKNOWN_OPTION MUST Each option an option reference, selection or key of cases names is one of its decision's INVALID_INSIGHT_REF MUST An option's insights name prior insights of its analysis OUTPUT_CYCLE MUST No output reads itself through inputs and cases, directly or not, pinned or not UNDECLARED_TEMPLATE_REF MUST Every brace of a command, read from the left, is in {{, }} or a placeholder UNDECLARED_TEMPLATE_REF MUST Placeholders are {inputs}, {output}, and {inputs.<entry>} or {decisions.<entry>} for entries as listed UNKNOWN_DERIVED_FROM MUST derived_from names a universe of its analysis, never an import DERIVED_FROM_CYCLE MUST No chain of derived_from loops back to its universe UNUSED_DECISION MUST A universe's own decisions set only decisions it uses on some branch INACTIVE_DECISION SHOULD Of the decisions it uses on some branch, a universe's own decisions set only those it uses MISSING_DECISION MUST An effective selection sets every decision its universe uses, of its analysis and of those its universes drive MISSING_REQUIRED_OPTION MUST An effective selection meets the requires of each option it selects for a decision in play INCOMPATIBLE_OPTIONS MUST An effective selection meets the incompatible_with of each option it selects for a decision in play EXCLUDED_OPTION_SELECTED MUST No effective selection selects an excluded option DUPLICATE_ELEMENT MUST No two keys of a universe's own decisions name one decision DUPLICATE_ELEMENT MUST A universe sets an inherited decision only under the key it inherits LOOPING_KEY MUST No universe key goes through a declaration that leads back UNKNOWN_PIN_UNIVERSE MUST Every pin names a universe: its analysis's entry or, lacking one, that of the analysis whose element its reference names PIN_NOT_BUILT MUST Every pinned output is built in the universe it is pinned to PIN_NOT_BUILT MUST Where a reached pin names a universe of an analysis other than the driving analysis, that universe sets each decision, of its analysis or one its universes drive, that what is reached through the pin uses there and it doesn't use itself validator, in each universe the driving analysis reaches NOT_BUILT_IN_UNIVERSE MUST Something reached reads another analysis's output built per universe, or its switch, or uses one of its decisions, only in a universe where that analysis is built UNDRIVEN_DECLARATION MUST In the file of a universe's analysis, every address by which something reached reads another analysis's output built per universe, or its switch, in that universe, or uses one of its decisions there, has a driven chain RESULT_IN_TWO_PLACES SHOULD No planned result has two names check MISSING_RECORD MUST Every planned result has a record at each of its places → missing INVALID_RECORD MUST The record at each place parses; its minor version has a record schema or exceeds the checker's → missing INVALID_RECORD MUST It meets that record schema or, if newer, the checker's open variant → missing MISPLACED_RECORD MUST Its address is the one its place is worked out from → missing MISSING_RECORD_INPUTS MUST Its inputs hold one item per entry its output lists at its commit, by entry, no more → missing STALE_RESULT MUST Nothing the result is made from has changed since its record's commit → stale ABSENT_RESULT SHOULD Its recorded bytes are at its default place, bar an unread result from a commit → absent STALE_EVIDENCE MUST Evidence citing a result cites an unchanged one → the result's record status runner UNRECORDED_RESULT MUST A runner writes each result it makes: a record at each place, bytes at each default place FALSE_RECORD MUST Every field of a record a runner writes is true of its run UNRECREATABLE_ENVIRONMENT MUST A runner records each recipe's environment as an IRI it can recreate at its version UNCOMMITTED_CHANGES MUST Each recipe runs in a commit's checkout changed only by records and recorded results UNCOMMITTED_CHANGES MUST There, untracked files and submodules count as changes; ignored files don't WRONG_WORKING_DIRECTORY MUST Each recipe runs in its own analysis's folder, even when driven NOT_AT_COMMIT MUST A runner drives an analysis from a commit on exactly its files at that commit REBUILT_FROM_COMMIT MUST A runner builds no result from a commit, and reads each through its record at its analysis's commit STALE_INPUT MUST A runner builds nothing from a result from a commit that is missing, stale or lacks its recorded bytes UNDECLARED_READ SHOULD A recipe reads input files and other results only through its output's inputs CODE_OUTSIDE_ANALYSIS SHOULD Beyond its environment, a recipe runs only code its inputs give, or tracked in its analysis's folder outside nested analyses

Recommendations and a permission that no tool checks:

Who Level Recommendation or permission A published analysis SHOULD declare only remotes its readers can fetch Branches that hold records SHOULD be merged, not squashed or rebased A runner SHOULD let someone see what an environment it recorded holds A runner MAY enforce UNDECLARED_READ and CODE_OUTSIDE_ANALYSIS, failing a recipe that breaks one

items.title: Schema files
items.text:
The schema is written in LinkML; its descriptions of the fields are published as the field reference. These files are generated from it, each at https://w3id.org/astra/<minor version>/<file>, shared by every patch of that minor version:

File What it is analysis.schema.json the JSON Schema (2019-09) of astra.yaml provenance.schema.json the JSON Schema of a record provenance.open.schema.json the same, but allowing fields it doesn't define, for records of a newer minor version provenance.context.jsonld the JSON-LD context that reads a record as W3C PROV-O rules.json every rule's code, layer, level and statement, and the code of each schema keyword whose error can fail a file

A file breaks no schema rule exactly when a JSON Schema 2019-09 validator reports no error for it against its schema.

name: AnalysisDeclaration

  `url`. Its elements are addressed through the declaration's id, as `<declaration>.<element>`.
from_schema: https://w3id.org/astra/analysis
attributes:
  id:
    name: id

      as its key in `analyses`.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/astra/analysis

    - Option

    required: true
  path:
    name: path
    annotations:
      rule:
        tag: rule
        value: INVALID_PATH
    description: The directory of the declared analysis's `astra.yaml`, relative to
      the folder of this `astra.yaml`, with `/` between folders. It is non-empty and
      doesn't start with `/`.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/astra/analysis
    owner: AnalysisDeclaration
    domain_of:
    - Input
    - AnalysisDeclaration
    range: string
    pattern: ^[^/]
  url:
    name: url
    annotations:
      rule:
        tag: rule
        value: INVALID_VALUE
    description: 'Where git fetches another repository from, as a remote with no ASCII
      space or control character, in one of two forms: `scheme://` and at least one
      character, where the scheme is an ASCII letter followed by any ASCII letters,
      digits, `+`, `.` and `-`, such as `https://example.org/remote.git` or `file:///srv/remote.git`;
      or scp-like, `[user@]host:path`, where `host`, `path` and any `user` are non-empty,
      `user` and `host` hold no `/`, `@` or `:`, and the value doesn''t start with
      a scheme and `://`, such as `git@example.org:remote.git`. The declared analysis
      is the one at the top level of that repository, at `commit`.'

    - AnalysisDeclaration

  commit:
    name: commit
    description: The full id of the commit the declared analysis is read at. A declaration
      with a `url` has one; with a `path`, it declares the analysis at that path as
      it was at that commit.

    rule:
      tag: rule
      value: URL_WITHOUT_COMMIT

      name: path
      required: true
- annotations:
    rule:

  slot_conditions:

      name: url
